10-1.title: What Are Living Things?
10-1.learn:
KEY IDEAS

Living things, or organisms, share certain features:
- They are made of CELLS.
- They USE ENERGY.
- They GROW and DEVELOP.
- They RESPOND to their surroundings.
- They REPRODUCE (make more of their kind).

The CELL is the basic building block of all living things. Some organisms are made of just ONE cell; others, like you, are made of TRILLIONS.

Scientists organize life from small to large: atoms → molecules → cells → tissues → organs → whole organisms.

Example 1 — Is it alive?
A dog is alive: it is made of cells, uses energy, grows, responds, and reproduces. A rock is NOT alive: it does none of these.

Example 2 — One cell vs. many
A bacterium is a single-celled organism; a human is made of trillions of cells.

Example 3 — Levels of organization
Cells make up tissues, tissues make up organs, and organs work together in a whole organism.

10-2.title: Classifying Living Things
10-2.learn:
KEY IDEAS

There are millions of kinds of living things, so scientists CLASSIFY (group) them by shared characteristics. This makes organisms easier to study and compare.

Scientists use the LINNAEAN system together with broad groups called DOMAINS to sort all life.

Each organism gets a two-part SCIENTIFIC NAME (genus + species) so people everywhere know exactly which living thing they mean — no matter what language they speak.

Example 1 — Why classify?
Grouping living things by shared traits (like having a backbone, or making their own food) makes them easier to study.

Example 2 — Scientific name
The two-part scientific name (like Homo sapiens for humans) is the same worldwide, avoiding confusion from common names.

Example 3 — Shared traits
Animals that have fur and feed milk to their young are grouped together because they share those characteristics.

10-3.title: Energy and Matter in Ecosystems
10-3.learn:
KEY IDEAS

An ecosystem is all the living and nonliving things in an area working together.

Energy flow: Energy enters most ecosystems from the SUN. Plants capture sunlight to make food, then animals eat the plants, and other animals eat those animals. This flow of energy from one living thing to the next is shown by FOOD CHAINS and FOOD WEBS.
- Producers (plants) make their own food using sunlight.
- Consumers (animals) eat other living things for energy.
- Decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil.

Matter (like water and nutrients) gets RECYCLED and used again and again.

Example 1 — Simple food chain
Sun → grass (producer) → rabbit (consumer) → fox (consumer). Energy flows from one to the next.

Example 2 — Producers vs. consumers
A plant is a producer (makes its own food); a deer is a consumer (eats plants).

Example 3 — Recycling matter
When a plant or animal dies, decomposers break it down and return its nutrients to the soil for new plants to use.

10-4.title: Microorganisms: Viruses, Bacteria, Protists, and Fungi
10-4.learn:
KEY IDEAS

Some living things are too small to see without a MICROSCOPE.
- Bacteria: tiny SINGLE-CELLED organisms found almost everywhere. Some are HELPFUL (like those that help digest food) and some are HARMFUL (cause disease).
- Protists: organisms like algae and amoebas.
- Fungi: organisms like mushrooms, mold, and yeast.
- Viruses: even SMALLER than bacteria and NOT quite alive — they can only reproduce by invading a living cell (a host).

Comparing these tiny agents helps us understand health and disease.

Example 1 — Bacteria can help or harm
Some bacteria help your body (like in your gut); others can make you sick.

Example 2 — Viruses need a host
A virus cannot reproduce on its own; it must invade a living cell to make copies of itself.

Example 3 — Match the microbe
Mold on bread = fungi. Algae in a pond = protist. The flu = caused by a virus.
